analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments first this morning in the National Labor Relations Board against the International Long Charmands Association. Mr. Cohn, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court. This case calls for this Court to review a second time the rules on containers, which are part of collective bargaining agreements between the International Longshoremen's Association and shipping industry employers on the Atlantic and Gulf Coast. The rules were adopted in response to a technological innovation in the shipping industry known as containerization, which has had an impact on Longshoremen's work. As this Court may recall, containers are large, reusable metal receptacles, 20 to 40 feet in length and capable of carrying upwards of 30,000 pounds of freight, which can be moved off an ocean vessel unopened. They can then be affixed to a truck chassis and transported intact to and from the pier like a trailer. The rules provide, in general, that if containers owned or leased by the shipping companies are to be unloaded or loaded, stripped or stuffed as the process is called in the industry, within 50 miles of the port. Anyone other than the beneficial owner of the cargo, the work must be done at the pier by longshoremen. The rules require shipping companies to deny containers to any facility operating in violation of the rules and to pay liquidated damages of $1,000 per container for any container handled in violation of the rules. Now, at first blush, the rules would appear to violate Section 80 of the National Labor Relations Act, which prohibits an employer in the union from agreeing that the employer will cease doing business with another person because they require the shipping companies to deny containers and thus do business with anyone operating in violation of the rules. But this court has held that 80 applies only to secondary activity and not to activity serving a legitimate primary purpose. And among the primary purposes protected by the Act is the purpose of preserving for the contracting employees themselves work traditionally done by them. On the other hand, decisions of this court have established that an agreement does not have a legitimate work preservation objective and is instead for a secondary objective that is unlawful under Section 80 if it seeks to acquire for union members work that was not previously theirs. Now, the last time this court, and what I shall refer to as ILA 1, this court vacated two decisions of the NLRB that had concluded that the rules on containers and their enforcement constituted secondary activity prescribed by Section 80 and 8B4B of the Labor Act. The court concluded that the court concluded that the court, in finding that the rules in their applications did not serve a valid work preservation objective, had applied an erroneous definition of the work in controversy, defining the disputed work as the container work performed by the truckers and consolidators at their off-peer premises after the innovation of containers, thereby foreclosing the longshoremen from playing any part in the loading or unloading of containerized cargo. So, the court accordingly remanded the case of the board to take another look at the rules, applying a proper definition of the work. And the court explained that the, or instructed the board, in determining whether the rules had a lawful work preservation object, to see whether they were tailored to the objective of preserving the essence of traditional work patterns. In short, the board was to undertake a careful analysis of the traditional work patterns that the rules were allegedly seeking to preserve, and determine whether the historical and functional relationship between this retained work and traditional longshore work could support the conclusion that the objective was work preservation rather than work acquisition. On remand, the board consolidated the two prior proceedings with seven other proceedings involving the rules, and after making the analysis which the court directed it to make of the traditional work patterns, concluded that the rules violated the Labor Act in their application to a widespread practice known as short-stopping and to certain traditional warehousing activities. These practices occur in connection with what is termed FSL container loads, which are containers holding import cargo, or export cargo, or import cargo destined for only one consignee, and export cargo from only one shipper. The board upheld the application of the rules that were at issue, insofar as they applied to less than container loads, which are containers holding export cargo from or import cargo destined to more than one shipper or consignee. The Court of Appeals, disagreeing with the board in part, held that the rules were lawful in their application to short-stopping and to the warehousing practices that the board found them to be unlawful. And this is the only aspect of the Court of Appeals decision which is now before this court. Mr. Cohn, is there anything in the board's opinion stating that loading and unloading before the short-stopping by truckers is not traditional longshoremen's work? Mr. Cohn, did you find anything to that effect in the opinion? Well, what the board did was to affirm the basic findings of the administrative law judge, except in two respects, which do not alter his finding that the short-stopping was not functionally related to traditional longshore work. That that was related to the work patterns of the motor carriers. So, uh, uh, by, uh, affirming the administrative law judge's findings and not rejecting, uh, this basic finding with respect to short-stopping, uh, uh, we submit that the board, uh, uh, did approve, uh, of the, uh, uh, administrative law judge's finding. Do you think that eliminated work, work that's eliminated because of technological change, can ever be preserved by a collective bargaining agreement? Mr. Cohn? I think that, uh, uh, that it may be possible in, in some circumstances. I think that, uh, uh, the board did not have to face that flat, uh, proposition because, in this case, the eliminated work that was sought to be, uh, replaced was, in the board's view and the administrative law judge's view, not work that was functionally, uh, related to traditional longshore work. It's an easier case where, uh, the employee seek to substitute for the eliminated work, work that is not functionally related to what they have been doing. And that is this case. Now, the hypothetical case that, uh, uh, your honor is positing as I, as I understand it, is, uh, uh, a situation where, uh, an effort is made to, uh, restore eliminated work that is, uh, uh, uh, uh, functionally related to work that had previously been performed. Uh, uh, as I say, the, the board did not have to, uh, come to grips with that, uh, uh, issue in this case. Uh, that will depend upon, uh, uh, uh, how one interprets, uh, national woodwork. Under, uh, uh, uh, uh, uh, one reading of that case, uh, uh, uh, it could lead to the conclusion that you could preserve. Well, the board appeared to rely on the fact that the work had been eliminated by technological change. Well, uh, uh, at least when I read it, that seemed to be what the board was talking about. Well, but, uh, your honor, I submit that what the board said, uh, uh, must, should be read in the light of the findings of the administrative law judge that the board did not disturb. Sure. And, and he, with respect to shortstopping, the situation is this. Prior to containerization, the cargo would be taken out of the hold of the ship by the longshoremen and put on the, uh, on the dock. It would then be loaded onto local trucks and carted to the motor carriers terminal. And loaded by whom, Mr. Cole? It would be loaded by longshoremen in some cases, in other cases by both longshoremen and truckers. That brake bulk, that initial brake bulk handling, has been eliminated as a result of containerization. Now, uh, but, uh, before containerization, uh, after it was loaded on the truck, it would be shortstopped. That's the point. And, or it would be warehoused. These very activities that go on now with containerization went on before. They went on before, and, as the board views it, what the longshoremen are trying to do is to substitute for that initial brake bulk handling that has been eliminated. The second handling that the motor carrier employees and the warehousemen had always done for purposes unrelated to longshore work. These are purposes that are related to, uh, uh, You mean to meet highway weight or, uh, That is correct, Your Honor. The first deal is the requirements. Or in the case of the warehousemen, to meet the demands of, uh, uh, of their customers, who say, store it and, uh, ship, uh, uh, 50 cartons. Or sometimes, I gather, for purposes of satisfying distribution. That, that is correct, Your Honor. And, uh, The board found that that work is not functionally related to traditional longshore work. That has always been part of the work patterns of the trucking employees and of the warehouse employees. And that the longshoremen, in seeking to claim that work, uh, are gone beyond the limited privilege given for, uh, attempting to preserve traditional work. Unlike the situation with the consolidation of less than container loads, Uh, where the board found that that work had merely moved from the pier to the consolidation terminal. The longshoremen at the pier itself. Uh, do any of us, uh, loading on the trucks to meet highway weight or safety require the truck? No, they do not. And as a matter of fact, uh, uh, you can't really determine whether you're going to, uh, uh, uh, have to do that until you get the thing to the, uh, to the terminal. Uh, the way the rules work, these full shipper load containers, they all go through. No, the longshoremen makes no claim to them as long as they go through, uh, to the ultimate consignee. The only, uh, uh, uh, uh, time that they, uh, uh, seek to grab hold of them is when they're being, uh, uh, uh, that is correct. And that work is not, uh, in the board's view, traditional longshore work. And so you think it's a really situation is really no different, uh, than if the, uh, the, the, was it FSL or? Yeah. If a full ship was loaded. Yeah. Uh, those containers go right through to the ultimate consignee within 50 miles. There's no claim to those. That is correct. And there shouldn't be on the same for the same reason. Well, that's right. Whether shortstop for reasons that are unrelated to, uh, uh, uh, uh, uh, purposes. I'd like to reserve the balance of my time for rebuttal. Mr. Lips. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it be a case like this where the primary secondary objective is found only by looking at whether or not the bargaining unit is seeking to acquire work as opposed to some other objectives. There are only two considerations, uh, that need be addressed. Uh, one is, um, uh, what is the traditional work? It's a disputed work in comparison with that work. And, where the work is of a different character and kind or type, uh, or, uh, or any word like that that connotes a change in form, then, technically speaking, none of that work relates to traditional work, because a traditional work of handling a bag at a time is no longer in existence. a traditional work of handling a bag at a time is no longer in existence. It's now unitized in a container. So technically speaking, none of the new work in its new form is related to the old work, and we argued last time we were here that that work can't be preserved. None of it can be preserved by the ILA. The court seems to have... Will you take the position that eliminated work can never be preserved? Eliminated work that, whether it's completely gone, obviously it can't be brought back, or if it changes form so that it's a new and different kind of work, then we take the none of it can be brought back. However, I recognize that ILA says, well, we can do it. We can just require it to be duplicated, make two people do the same thing twice. Well, what is it that they're talking about? They are saying that they can require duplicate work on the pier by unloading the container, but unloading the container is the new form of work. That's not the traditional work. Handling brake bulk cargo was a traditional work. Your position last time. Exactly, sir. What I believe you said was that... We thought that the work that they were claiming was just moving somewhere else. The suggestion that I believe you said was that that portion of the new work that is related to the old work may be preserved, but that portion that's not related because it serves a different transportation purpose or function cannot be preserved. Because what I believe the court said, and what we believe this case to be about is, that you can't just decide this case by virtue of examining physical skills of handling cargo a piece at a time. Because both sides have handled this cargo traditionally for years like that, as Hormat said, from the dawn of time. What we say here is that we're dealing with a new form of work. And because purpose relates to function, then the purpose of this work is related to motor transportation. At least this portion, short-stopping portion, is beyond the traditional function of ILA labor. ...the logical rule of the 50-mile limit. There is none, sir. It's totally arbitrary. And what... ...at least as well be 10 miles or 1,000 miles, you think? I believe you're right. And what judgment... I'm not suggesting a conclusion. I'm putting it as a question. I agree that it's totally arbitrary and has no functional relation to the traditional interplay of the work. Now, neither you nor your friend have used the word feather bedding. Is this something like feather bedding? I believe it is exactly feather bedding, your honor, in some sense. Not necessarily entirely, because we... It's like putting two engineers or two oilers on a vessel where only one is needed, is it? Quite. That is true. Only where the work is actually duplicated. In most cases, in this case, if the work is done on the pair, it will not be duplicated by any employer within the 50-mile zone whom we represent, because the work will be diverted beyond the 50-mile zone. The undisputed evidence in the record is to that effect. Shippers and consignees are not going to have this work done twice. It makes no economic sense, and they won't do it. So our warehousemen, who have hundreds of thousands of dollars of warehouses in the piers that they can't move beyond the 50 miles, are going to dry up and die. And our motor carriers, who are local carriage carriers within the 50-mile zones, are not going to have anything to do, because shippers simply will not pay to have the work duplicated. One thing you need to understand factually is, shortstop work is done at the cost of the motor carrier for his convenience. This work, full shippers' load work, is paid for on a transportation basis from point of origin to point of ultimate destination. There are no charges levied for the unloading of that cargo by transportation companies. When the ILA stops at work at the period, it adds on unloading charges. When the ILA releases that work, as it has done according to the rules, and lets it go wherever it's going to go without unloading, but then the motor carrier shortstops the work, no additional charges are charged to the consignee or shipper, because the motor carrier is sustaining the cost of that unloading for economic reasons related to his own business. And that serves a trucker's function, which has nothing to do with traditional maritime transportation functions. I gather the Court of Appeals thought that if the result was duplicative work, inefficient handling and so forth, that's not a problem for us, but for the Congress, didn't it? I believe that the Court of Appeals misunderstood... No, but that's what the Court of Appeals thought, wasn't it, no? I haven't grasped the essence of your statement then, because I misunderstand what you're... No, that if the consequence of all this is that the longshoremen are right, and you negotiate your own work preservation agreement, and there's duplicative work that's done twice, as Justice O'Connor suggested, didn't the Fourth Circuit seem to think that was a problem to be resolved by the Congress and not by the courts? Well, I'll try to answer the question as I understand it. We believe the Fourth Circuit misunderstood the facts to begin with. There will not be duplicative work. There's no such holding in the decision. There's no such evidence to support such a conclusion. Secondly, that element, that discussion by the Fourth Circuit as to whether or not there would be work acquisition, transfer of work back to the peer or not, is simply a surrounding circumstance that may bear on whether or not there's a functional relationship, but the transfer of work is only a circumstance, and the Court used it as an ultimate legal test. We think the established law is clear that actual work transfer is not an element of secondary objective. Now, whether or not in the Congress's wisdom it believes that by making the transfer of work an element of secondary activity is a good thing to do, I don't know. I suggest simply that that standard applied by the Court of Appeals was merely a circumstance that really is not dispositive of the functional relationship. Thank you very much. Mr. Caruso? Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, we have heard argument from the opponents of the Rules and we have had the opportunity to review their briefs. Mr. Chief Justice, and essentially what they are saying, their entire case, rests on the proposition that the Board can't write English and the Fourth Circuit can't read it. They take the position that the Board made a finding that the work involved in stripping or stuffing containers as assigned by the rules in the context of short-stopping and warehousing is not functionally and historically related to longshore work. The Board never made that finding. It is clear that the Board, but it is clear that the Board, it is clear that the administrative law, just plainly, three times in its decision, three times it held and found that the work involved there is functionally and historically related to longshore work. On page 54 of the appendix that was submitted with the petitions for certiorari, the Board states, it is clear that the administrative law judge considered the work claimed by this rule to be functionally related to the traditional work of longshoremen in loading and unloading cargo on and off a ship for ocean transport. The same statement is made on page 53. The same finding is made on pages 58 to 59. The Board's Council takes the position that this statement is only in connection with consolidation work, that context in which the Board upheld the rules. But the statement I just read is in a portion of the NLRB's decision that has the title short-stopping. It is plain that the Board found the functional and historical relationship. Well, I don't think there's any argument that what the four containers, the longshoremen were surely handling cargo at the pier, even though it was later short-stopped or warehoused. Surely, what the longshoremen are trying to do is to be paid for that work that has been eliminated. But what about the work that was done before containers? What about the work that was done by the trucking people in short-stopping and by the warehousing people in their warehousing operations? What about that work? Was that related to longshoremen's activity or not? No, it wasn't. But that's not the work that the rules seek to assign, just this way. Well, just bear with me. I just want to know whether you agree or not that that work was or was it not related to longshoremen's work. The off-peer enterprises unloaded trucks, and then they performed a variety of tasks, segregating cargo, palletizing cargo in connection with loading over-the-road equipment or warehousing. And they're still doing that after containers, yes. And if the rules on containers are applied, they still do that work. That's the point that the Fourth Circuit made. The Fourth Circuit recognized that, that you can't have acquisition without acquisition. In order for our adversaries to prevail, they have to have a factual basis upon which to conclude. Don't you think that work is going to be done outside the 50-mile limit from now on? I don't think it will, because we talk about the 50-mile range. You mean the shippers are going to put up with being charged twice for this business? There's two answers to that, just as well. The first one is, in the past, I'll strike that, in connection with the reasons for short-stopping, our adversaries tell us that there is a need not to have an empty container moving back to the pier. There's a need to have equipment that's compatible with containers. All of those reasons also dictate that if the rules are applied, the worker's not going to go outside 50 miles, for the same reasons that they say that the container is being short-stopped. Those same reasons apply. But the more important element, from a legal standpoint, is that in order for these rules to be unlawful, Congress has told us what the test is. This court has reiterated the test. There has to be a showing that it says a secondary objective. There cannot be a secondary objective in that situation, because the longshoremen aren't getting anything. If the work went outside the 50-mile range, the rules say that those containers may move intact, without any work being performed by the longshoremen. Certainly the longshoremen have no objective to lose work. They want to bring back to the peers the work that they've always traditionally performed. The basis for the NLRB's decision was, well, this work has been eliminated as a necessary consequence. On that basis, I suppose, if that was a valid reason for ruling against you, I suppose it would have been a valid reason with respect to the consolidators. I think that would probably be a fair conclusion to draw, but it isn't a valid reason. We didn't think so either, apparently, in the last time. Well, it seems obvious to me that, you know, that the word eliminated means that the work that the longshoremen has done in the past has been eliminated. It's their work. Now, to acquire your own work is preservation. It's not acquisition. When you say it's their work, you mean by tradition it was work that they performed? Well, it's work that's functionally and historically related to their traditional work. Obviously, no one stripped the stuffed containers when containers didn't exist, but there was the cargo handling functions in connection with the loading and unloading of the vessel, and those functions still exist. That container is the container owned by my clients, the employers of the longshoremen. It is their equipment. That container has to be unloaded in order for the cargo to be delivered as part of my client's obligation to see to it that the cargo is transported. What do you suggest is the function of the 50-mile limit instead of 35 or 65? Well, it's a rule. The contention is made that it's going to run, that it's an arbitrary rule because all the work is now going to fly out past the 50-mile range. There's no evidence in this record that there's anyone out there on the 50-yard line. There just isn't any evidence. The evidence indicates that the truckers, that the warehousemen, that the consolidators are clustered around the piers. All they're doing is taking that container, moving it several blocks down from the pier just for the purpose of unloading it. That's the work that the longshoremen have done in the past. So you think they're really doing something besides historic shortstopping? Well, to the extent... You think they're doing something now after containers that they weren't doing before? They're unloading the container. Well, they did before. The containers have their equipment. I know, but they used to unload the trucks. Yes, and if the rules are applied, they will continue to unload the trucks. And then reload, and then reload. And then reload their over-the-road equipment. The only thing is they're unloading containers now rather than the truck. Yes, but the difference there, of course, is that in the past the truck was owned by their employer, and now the container is owned by my clients who employ the longshoremen. It's a very important difference. It's a difference that really has a significance in the so-called right of control area. That's not an issue that's before us today. What is the difference in the overall economic sense? Well, from my perspective, the Board seems to be taking the unspoken position that it's going to be more economical if the rules are invalidated. From my client's perspective, we don't see that. If the rules are invalidated, we have an obligation under federal labor law to sit down at a bargaining table and bargain with the union over some new means of preserving their work. That's going to be costly. During the ten years that these rules have been enjoined on what have been found to be errors of law, my clients have suffered because we had to come up with something else. And that something else was costly. So from an economic standpoint... Something else. What is the something else? Well, I don't want to give any sort of a hint to my colleague here who represents the union as to what he should come up with at the bargaining table. I'd prefer not to get into that area. I think he's perfectly capable of coming up with the something else. Perhaps he'll explain it to us. So when you analyze the Board's decision, you find that the Board found and answered the questions posed by this Court in ILA 1. Namely, that the work at issue in the shore stopping and wareharing context is functionally and historically related to traditional longshore work. They also found that that work, that stripping and stuffing work, is not integrated into any of the off-peer work practices. Absent that integration, when the stuffing and stripping required by the rules is performed at the peers, there's no possibility for any off-peer work to be acquired by the longshoremen because the long... The stuffing and stripping work is not integrated with any of that work. If there were integration, then the ruling would have been different. But there wasn't any integration. On that basis, they concluded that the rules have a lawful work preservation objective. Then they attempted to invalidate the rules on the basis of a proposition or theory that an attempt to preserve or retain eliminated work constitutes work acquisition. The court of appeals readily corrected that error. In order to have acquisition, there has to be a transfer of work. Well, let me ask you how the rule operates. Doesn't the rule forbid the employer... Doesn't the union require the employer to cease doing business with anybody who unloads one of these containers within 50 miles? Well... Yes or no? I'd say no. It depends on how you define cease doing business. The business still continues. It's just a question of not releasing the container. What the rules require is that the cargo be brought to the peer loose. Well, you won't... You won't... It requires the employer not to furnish a container to a trucking company who shortstops within 50 miles. If the trucking company shortstops, then the sanction is not to release a container to that company. Well, that's a... Unless the company... Unless the company... Unless the company... Well, that certainly is a form of ceasing, requiring somebody to cease doing business. Well, it's... You cease doing... Renting them a container or paying. Isn't that right? Our... Our perspective is, in order to determine whether it is a cessation of business, one doesn't look at it today after 10 years of injunctions. Well, let me... Let me put it... Put it another way. If a... A trucking company must not shortstop if the rules are to be obeyed. No. No. And it may not shortstop with the container. Yes, it can... It can continue to shortstop, continue to warehouse, but if it's going to be done, they should inform us, and they should bring their truck down to the pier and pick up the cargo, as was the traditional method of doing that. So... So the answer is, they may not shortstop with the container. That's basically correct. And so... But the business doesn't... It seems to me that the rules, then, do have an impact off the pier. Oh, I... It does. It certainly... It certainly prevents these trucking companies from shortstopping if they have a container. They can continue to shortstop, but without utilizing my client's container. That's correct. Now, that may be an impact, but we contend that's an ancillary effect of a primary work preservation agreement of their... So, containerization... Containers can play no part in shortstopping. They have to... Use their own equipment. They have to come down to the pier and pick the stuff up loose in their truck just like they used to. And that's a continuation of business the way it used to be performed. Exactly. So there's no cessation of business. Exactly. It's business as usual. Exactly. Business as usual and it won't be any more expensive. It shouldn't be any more expensive. In fact, they contend that the container is expensive because they've got to send the container back to the pier. Because they don't want to encode per diem charges. They don't want to have to hold that container empty back to the pier. So I think the effect is certainly exaggerated by my adversaries. But I think one of the important elements from our standpoint is the effect of permitting the board by administrator fiat to in effect change the law of Congress that Congress enacted. When we negotiated this bargain, it would have been our preference as businessmen not to have to deal with these rules, not to agree to the rules. But Congress said we must bargain and Congress said that the union has a right to preserve work. We sat down and we bargained. As we understood the law, we were engaged in a perfectly lawful activity. Now the board is attempting to pervert the meaning of words like acquisition and elimination and to come up with a conclusion in which perfectly primary activity is now giving a secondary taint. The effect is, unlike a situation where Congress enacts a law which has a prospective application, this is going to have a retroactive application, a retrospective application. And it's going to place my clients in the position of having to answer potential claims, possibly under the antitrust laws for treble damages and also other damage type of claims of substantial sums of money on the basis of action that we took 15 years ago, which at that time we considered and still consider to be perfectly lawful activity. It's primary activity. It's primary activity. If there's going to be a change in the law, then it should be done prospectively. It should be done by Congress. Well, the act of Congress certainly doesn't help your clients here. It's the National Woodworking case in which this court upheld the board. Reading the act of Congress as written, I think your clients would be in very great difficulty. And the board supported the view you take in National Woodworking. Now it takes a different view. There's no reason why the board can't shift its position. Which I think Congress indicated in 1959 by the enactment of the primary proviso, that's where Congress indicated that even though there may be a cessation of business, and even though there may be an agreement to agree to cease doing business, if it's for a primary purpose, it's perfectly lawful. And we submit that this is for a primary purpose, and the board is attempting by Administrator Fiat to convert it into something secondary just by affixing that label and calling it secondary, on the basis of the fact that the work has been eliminated.
